newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil sets third new auction date for CVRD sale.
newsitem.headline: Brazil sets third new auction date for CVRD sale.

text.p: Brazil Friday rescheduled for the third time the auction of state-owned mining giant Companhia Vale do Rio Doce (CVRD) in a legal battle that local media have likened to one of the country's famous soap operas.

The privatisation, now set for May 5, had been programmed for May 2 but was scrapped after a high court judge said he would not rule before May 5 on a government appeal against a number of court injunctions blocking the sale.
Latin America's largest privatisation to date had originally been scheduled for April 29. But the auction was delayed first to April 30, then May 2 and now May 5 due to a slew of court injunctions.

Justice Democrito Ramos Reinaldo from the Superior Court of Justice (STJ) is now considering whether he will accept the government's request that all lawsuits against the CVRD sale should be handled by a single tribunal.
He told reporters Thursday he would examine the case over the weekend and Monday may have a decision.
The ongoing saga was summed up by one of Rio de Janeiro's leading newspapers Friday. Its business section carried the headline "CVRD auction turns into a soap opera".
An STJ decision in the government's favour would allow the government to try and quickly overturn injunctions granted by several different courts.
If the sell-off cannot take place Monday, the auction will be rescheduled for each subsequent day during a period of possibly 10 days, a Planning Ministry spokeswoman said.

More than 120 lawsuits have been filed against the company's privatisation, a record compared with the number of cases against the sell-off of steelmaker Usiminas, the first of Brazilian state companies to be privatised six years ago.

Seen as a key test to President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's commitment to reform the economy, the sale of CVRD, considered the biggest in Latin America to date, has mobilised considerable opposition from nationalists and leftists.
Opponents, from former presidents Itamar Franco and Jose Sarney to Brazil's Roman Catholic bishops, have accused the government of selling the country's mineral wealth to foreigners for a pittance.
The company's Carajas mine is the biggest iron ore deposit in the world with reserves of 15 billion tons.
With the sale of a maximum 45 percent voting stake in CVRD, the government expects to raise at least $2.8 billion. If completed, the firm's privatisation could net the government about $5.0 billion.

Two groups are ready to bid for the control of the miner: one led by local steel firm CSN, and another headed by Brazil's largest private industrial conglomerate Grupo Votorantim and South Africa's Anglo-American Corp.
